title: The frontal defence
summary: King cut off from the pawn: the rook goes in front of it, checks from the front or offers itself for a trade.
part.front.title: Checks from the front
part.front.summary: The king cut off, the rook on the first rank and the checks the black king cannot escape.
part.back.title: Check or go back
part.back.summary: The black king touches the pawn: check. It steps away: the rook goes back in front of the pawn. It abandons it: capture.
part.first.title: Rook first
part.first.summary: When the rook is far away, it gets back to the first rank before the king moves. Tal against Zaitsev, 1968.
part.king.title: Where the king stands
part.king.summary: Your king close to the cutting file, ready to attack the black rook. Arencibia against Vladimirov, 1991.
part.trade.title: The rook trade
part.trade.summary: When the checks are not enough, the rook offers itself. And the rule of three: when the pawn is already too close.
part.side.title: The cut along the rank
part.side.summary: Pawn on its fifth rank and no trade: the rook separates the black king from the pawn along the rank. Pein against Ward, 1997.
part.recap.title: Summary
part.recap.summary: The rules of the frontal defence and the practical challenge.
step.t_front: The black king is on h5, next to its pawn, and the black rook on f7 cuts your king off: it cannot cross to the f-file. You defend with White. How do you hold this pawn?
step.t_front.hint1: Your rook is far from the pawn, on the first rank. That distance is a weapon.
step.t_front.hint2: The black king wants to escape the check without leaving its pawn. From where can the rook check so that the king can never get close to it?
step.intro: This is the frontal defence, in the textbook position from John Emms. Your king is cut off and cannot get in front of the pawn. The rook does the defending: it stands on the first rank, in front of the pawn, and checks from the front. Look at the three empty squares between the rook and the pawn: g4, g3 and g2. That is the rule of three. With that much distance, the black king can neither approach the rook nor hide behind its pawn.
step.d_checks: Watch the checks. The black king tries to come forward and the rook will not let it.
step.d_checks.m1: 1.Rh1+. A check from the front, along the h-file. The king has to move.
step.d_checks.m2: 1...Kg4: the king steps in front of its own pawn, the most ambitious square. From there it wants to come down to the rook.
step.d_checks.m3: 2.Rg1+. Now along the g-file. In front of the pawn, the king gets checked too.
step.d_checks.m4: 2...Kh4: back to the h-file, still touching the pawn.
step.d_checks.m5: 3.Rh1+. The king went back to h4 and gets the same check as before: in three moves it has not advanced a single square.
step.d_checks.m6: 3...Kg3: the king comes down, trying to reach the rook.
step.d_checks.m7: 4.Rg1+. And it never ends: the pawn cannot advance while the king is in check, and the king cannot reach the rook, which is far away.
step.checks: Your turn. Give the checks from the front. And watch out: if the black king abandons the pawn to escape, the rook takes it.
step.checks.hint: 1.Rh1+, then 2.Rg1+. If the king goes to h3, the pawn on g5 is left undefended.
step.checks.done: The king ran to h3 and the pawn fell. A draw. That is what happens when the king gets tired of the checks.
step.t_back: In the previous part the black king stayed glued to its pawn. Now it also tries to step away. The pawn is a bishop pawn on c5, still on its fourth rank. Your rook is on c1, in front of it, and the black rook on d7 cuts your king off along the d-file. The black king on b4 wants to go to c4 and push the pawn, and waiting here loses. What do you play, and how do you go on depending on where the black king goes?
step.t_back.hint1: The black king is right next to the pawn. What forces it to leave?
step.t_back.hint2: If it steps away from the pawn, look at who still defends the pawn on c5.
step.backWhy: The rule is one question every move: did the black king touch the pawn or step away? It touched it: check, to drive it off. It stepped away: the rook goes back to the c-file, in front of the pawn, and attacks the pawn, which is now undefended. It abandoned it for good: the rook captures. Here the king is touching the pawn, so the check comes first, 1.Rb1+.
step.d_back: Watch the question, move by move.
step.d_back.m1: 1.Rb1+. The king is touching the pawn: check along the b-file, to drive it away.
step.d_back.m2: 1...Ka3: the king gets out of check, but it steps away, and the pawn on c5 is left undefended.
step.d_back.m3: 2.Rc1! No check. The rook goes back in front of the pawn and threatens 3.Rxc5.
step.d_back.m4: 2...Kb4: the king comes back to defend the pawn and, by doing so, touches it again.
step.d_back.m5: 3.Rb1+. It touched the pawn, so check: the same question, the same answer.
step.d_back.m6: 3...Ka5: the king steps away again, now to a5, and the pawn on c5 is undefended once more.
step.d_back.m7: 4.Rc1. It stepped away, so back it goes: the rook attacks the pawn again, and the black king has to come back to defend it. The question repeats every move: a draw.
step.backError: And what if you wait? After 1.Kf3? c4! the pawn reaches its fifth rank: only c3 and c2 are left between the rook and the pawn. The checks still come, 2.Rb1+ Ka3 3.Rc1, but 3...Kb3 defends the pawn, and the rook is too close to drive the king away. The frontal defence is over.
step.backPlay: Now you, in the same position. The black king will choose other squares. Every move, the question: it touched the pawn, check; it stepped away, the rook goes back in front of the pawn; it abandoned it, capture.
step.backPlay.hint: Start with 1.Rb1+. Then look where the king went: next to the pawn or away from it?
step.backPlay.done: Check, back, check, and the pawn fell. A draw.
step.t_tal: Up to now your rook was already on the first rank. What if it is far away? Mikhail Tal, with White, against Igor Zaitsev, Soviet Team Cup, Riga, 1968. After 70.Kxa4 Rf4+, Zaitsev won back the g4 pawn with 71...Rxg4, and a knight pawn was left, on g6. The black rook on e4 cuts your king off along the e-file, and your rook is on b5. With 72...Re4, Zaitsev let the win slip: now only one move draws. Which one?
step.t_tal.hint1: Both the king and the rook want to move. Look at what the black rook does after each of them.
step.t_tal.hint2: Think about what the black rook wants to take away from you, and what your rook would lose because of it.
step.tal: Tal played 73.Kd3?? The idea was to bring the king first. Zaitsev replied 73...Re1! The black rook took the first rank, and your rook can no longer get in front of the pawn. After that, no white move holds, and Tal resigned on the spot.
step.d_talRight: Now the move that drew, from the game position.
step.d_talRight.m1: 73.Rb1! The rook first, while the first rank is still free. Now the first rank is yours: the black rook can no longer occupy it.
step.d_talRight.m2: 73...g5. The pawn moves, but the rook gets in front of it in time.
step.d_talRight.m3: 74.Kd3. Now it is the king's turn, towards the e-file and the black rook.
step.d_talRight.m4: 74...Re5. The black rook defends the pawn from the side, so that the black king can advance.
step.d_talRight.m5: 75.Kd4. The king attacks the rook and gains a tempo: it has to move.
step.d_talRight.m6: 75...Re8. The rook retreats without leaving the e-file: the cut stays.
step.d_talRight.m7: 76.Rg1. The rook in front of the pawn, with three squares between them, and the king close to the e-file. The frontal defence is set up: a draw.
step.knight: Tal's pawn was a knight pawn, and against it the frontal defence holds even with the king cut off by two files: on the far side of the pawn there is only the a-file, and the black king has nowhere to hide from the checks. Chéron showed this in 1923. With a bishop pawn at the same distance, the black king has room on both sides and the defence loses. The order of danger: bishop pawn, then centre pawn, then knight pawn.
step.getFront: Now you. A knight pawn, your king cut off by two files, and your rook on c1, not in front of the pawn. Rook first, in front of the pawn; checks after.
step.getFront.hint: 1.Rb1. Then 2.Ra1+ when the king goes to a5, 3.Rb1+ when it goes to b4, and 4.Rc1+ when it goes to c4.
step.getFront.done: The black king walks from side to side and the pawn does not move. A draw.
step.t_aren: In Tal's correct line, 75.Kd4 already showed the king attacking the black rook. Now that is the main move. Walter Arencibia, with White, against Evgeny Vladimirov, Leon, 1991. After 67.Rxa5 Rd1+ 68.Ke2 Rd6, rook against rook and bishop pawn was left. The pawn is on c6, the black rook on d6 cuts your king off along the d-file, and your king is on e2. Only one move draws. Which one?
step.t_aren.hint1: The rook does not need to move now. Look at the king.
step.t_aren.hint2: The king helps when it can get close to the black rook and attack it.
step.aren: Arencibia played 69.Rc5? The idea was to put the rook in front of the pawn. It was too early: with the king on e2, far from the squares where it would attack the black rook, Vladimirov replied 69...Kb4! The black king attacks the rook and goes to the side of the pawn. Then came 70.Rc1 c5 71.Rb1+ Ka3 72.Rc1 Rd5: the black rook defends the pawn from the side, your king cannot get there to attack it, and Arencibia resigned.
step.d_arenRight: Now the move that drew, from the game position.
step.d_arenRight.m1: 69.Ke3! The king steps up to e3, right next to the d-file. From there it reaches e4, the square from which it attacks the black rook when it defends the pawn along the fifth rank.
step.d_arenRight.m2: 69...Kb4. The black king comes to the side of the pawn, as in the game.
step.d_arenRight.m3: 70.Ra1. The rook goes to the first rank, from where it gives the checks.
step.d_arenRight.m4: 70...c5. The pawn moves, with the king beside it.
step.d_arenRight.m5: 71.Rb1+. The king is touching the pawn: check.
step.d_arenRight.m6: 71...Ka3. The king gets out of check and steps away from the pawn.
step.d_arenRight.m7: 72.Rc1. It stepped away: the rook goes back in front of the pawn and attacks it.
step.d_arenRight.m8: 72...Rd5. The black rook defends the pawn from the side, as in the game.
step.d_arenRight.m9: 73.Ke4! Now the king arrives in time. It attacks the rook, and the pawn is about to lose its defender.
step.d_arenRight.m10: 73...Rd4+. The rook leaves with check, protected by the pawn on c5.
step.d_arenRight.m11: 74.Ke3! The only move: the king steps back without leaving the d-file and attacks the rook again. On e5, 74...Kb4 brings the black king to the pawn; on f3 or f5, 74...c4 and the pawn moves on. A draw.
step.farKing: Arencibia's mistake again, in a cleaner form: the king too far away. Here your king is on c2, and your rook is already on the first rank. If it goes straight in front of the pawn, 1.Rg1?, Black plays 1...Rd7 and cuts your king off by one more file: then there is no defence. In Riga it was the other way round, because the first rank was in danger. Here it is already yours, and the king comes first.
step.far: King first, rook after. Your move.
step.far.hint: 1.Kd3. Then 2.Rh1+ and 3.Rg1+ as the black king moves.
step.far.done: The king arrived in time and the checks do the rest. A draw.
step.t_emms: Up to now the rook held with the help of the king. Sometimes the best thing it can do is leave the board. Now the pawn is a bishop pawn. The rook is in front, your king cut off along the e-file. Your move. More than one move holds, and one of them ends the cut at once. Which one?
step.t_emms.hint1: Imagine Black were to move. Where would the black king go?
step.t_emms.hint2: Sometimes the best square for the rook is one where it can be traded. Think about the king and pawn ending that would be left.
step.emms: If Black were to move here, 1...Kg5! would win. With a bishop pawn the black king has more room to hide from the checks, and when they run out the black rook comes to e5 to guard the pawn from the side. The king steps out of the way and the pawn rolls down. The position is from Emms. With White to move, three moves hold: 1.Rg1, the rook in front of the pawn; 1.Kd3, bringing the king closer; and 1.Re1!, offering the trade, which ends the cut at once. Let's look at the trade.
step.d_emms.m1: 1.Re1! The rook offers itself on the cutting file, facing the black rook.
step.d_emms.m2: 1...Rxe1. Black accepts. If Black declined by moving the rook off the e-file, the cut would be gone and your king would come close to the pawn.
step.d_emms.m3: 2.Kxe1. The cut is gone: king and pawn against king is left.
step.d_emms.m4: 2...Ke5. The black king comes next to its pawn, on its way to e4.
step.d_emms.m5: 3.Kf1! The king waits on the first rank, ready to take the opposition when the black king comes down. 3.Kf2? loses, because after 3...Kf4! it is the black king that has the opposition.
step.d_emms.m6: 3...Ke4. The black king comes down, aiming for e3, f3 or g3, two ranks ahead of the pawn: from there the pawn would get through.
step.d_emms.m7: 4.Ke2! The opposition: the kings face each other with one square between them, and Black is to move. It cannot get through. A drawn pawn ending.
step.rule3: And when even the checks do not work? Here the pawn has come down one more square, and only g3 and g2 are left between it and your rook. With Black to move, Black wins: the black king shelters next to its pawn, and the rook, too close, has no room for checks. It is the rule of three the other way round. With the pawn on its fifth rank, the frontal defence is over.
step.five: Same position, but now it is your move. Checks will not save you. One thing does.
step.five.hint: 1.Rf1: offer the trade. Then 2.Kxf1 and, when the black king comes, 3.Kg2.
step.five.done: King on g2, in front of the pawn: the black king cannot get past. A draw. The trade only works because your king was right there to recapture.
step.t_side: In the previous part, with the pawn on its fifth rank, only the trade saved you. Here even that does not exist: the black rook is far from yours. The pawn is a centre pawn on d4, already on its fifth rank; the black rook on e8 cuts your king off along the e-file, and the black king is on c6. Your rook is on a1, and putting it in front of the pawn loses. What holds?
step.t_side.hint1: The pawn cannot promote on its own: it needs the black king beside it.
step.t_side.hint2: Your rook can stand between the black king and the pawn.
step.sideWhy: The frontal defence needs three squares between the rook and the pawn, and here only d3 and d2 would be left. So the rook changes its job: instead of checking, it separates the black king from the pawn, with 1.Ra5, along the fifth rank. The pawn comes down alone, and your king, right next to the e-file, takes care of the rest.
step.sideError: First, see what happens with the rook in front. After 1.Rd1? Kc5! the black king comes to the side of the pawn, and your king cannot cross the e-file. It would go 2.Kf2 Kc4 3.Rc1+ Kd3: the king gets in front of the pawn, and the rook is too close for checks.
step.d_side: Now the cut along the rank, move by move.
step.d_side.m1: 1.Ra5! The rook cuts the black king off along the fifth rank: it cannot cross to b5, c5 or d5.
step.d_side.m2: 1...d3. The pawn comes down alone, without its king.
step.d_side.m3: 2.Kf2! The king comes closer to the pawn, right next to the e-file. From there it watches e1 and e2, the squares the black rook would use to help the pawn.
step.d_side.m4: 2...d2. The pawn is one square from promoting.
step.d_side.m5: 3.Ra1! The rook goes back to the first rank and watches d1, the promotion square.
step.d_side.m6: 3...Kc5. Only now does the black king come, but the rook has done its job: it is far away.
step.d_side.m7: 4.Rd1! The rook goes in front of the pawn, stuck on d2. Your king covers e1 and e2, and the black king arrives too late. A draw.
step.peinWard: The cut does not always save you. Malcolm Pein against Chris Ward, British Championship, Hove, 1997. After 57.Rxd5 Kxf7, rook against rook and bishop pawn was left. Here the pawn is already on c3, and Pein played 65.Rh5, cutting the black king off along the fifth rank, as you have just seen. But the pawn was two files beyond the e-file, where the black rook held Pein's king on f3, and the king could not arrive in time. After 65...c2 66.Rh1 Rc7, the black king walked down to b2, and Pein resigned after 70...Kb2. The cut along the rank needs your king close to the pawn.
step.sidePlay: Now you, with the black king trying another route. The rook cuts along the rank, and the king stays right next to the e-file.
step.sidePlay.hint: Start with 1.Ra5. Then 2.Kf2 and, when the pawn moves, 3.Ra3, attacking it from the side.
step.sidePlay.done: The black king stayed on the far side of the rook, and the pawn cannot get through on its own. A draw.
step.t_quick: Before the practical challenge, put it all together. A knight pawn, the black rook cuts your king off along the f-file, your king is on d2 and your rook on e1, not in front of the pawn. Which rule applies here, and what is the first move?
step.t_quick.hint1: First ask whether each piece is in its place.
step.t_quick.hint2: Remember the order from the lesson: what has to be ready before the checks?
step.recap: Three rules. One: the rook on the first rank before the black rook takes it, and in front of the pawn, with three squares between them; then check when the black king touches the pawn, go back in front when it steps away, capture when it abandons it. Two: your king close to the cutting file, ready to attack the black rook when it defends the pawn from the side; if the black rook could cut it off by one more file, the king comes before the rook. Three: with the pawn on its fifth rank, offer the trade if the pawn ending is a draw; otherwise, cut the black king off along the rank. Here the first one applies: 1.Rg1.
step.when: And when do you use it? When your king is cut off from the pawn and the pawn has not yet passed its fourth rank. Against a knight pawn the defence holds with the king cut off by two files; against a bishop or centre pawn, only by one, and not always.
step.quick: Now play the position. It is the last one before the practical challenge.
step.quick.hint: 1.Rg1, in front of the pawn. Then the checks, and 4.Rxg5 if the king abandons the pawn.
step.quick.done: Rook in front, checks, and the pawn fell. A draw.
step.finish: Now the practical challenge. Rook in front of the pawn, checks from the front, and the trade when the pawn ending is a draw.
ex.e11: White to play and draw. Your rook is far away on the eighth rank, and the black rook cuts your king off along the f-file. Only one move holds.
ex.e11.hint: A check from behind does not scare this king. Where does the rook hold a knight pawn?
ex.e11.solution: 1.Ra1! The rook goes back to the first rank, in front of the pawn, and from there the checks never end: 1...Kg4 2.Rg1+, 2...Kh4 3.Rh1+. 1.Rh8+? loses: the black king hides and the pawn moves. Position from emanuelrigelnuma's study.
ex.e12: White to play and draw. From Capablanca's analysis: the pawn has reached its fourth rank and your rook is on h2, not in front of it. The checks lose.
ex.e12.hint: Two ideas hold: drive the black rook off the d-file, or allow the pawn ending, which is a draw.
ex.e12.solution: 1.Rd2, offering the trade: after 1...Rxd2 2.Kxd2, your king gets in front of the pawn. 1.Kc2, attacking the rook, also holds. 1.Re2+? or 1.Rh6+? lose: the black king walks out of the checks and the pawn advances with the black rook cutting your king off. Capablanca's analysis.
ex.e08: White to play and draw. A bishop pawn on its fifth rank, your king cut off along the d-file. The rook in front of the pawn no longer works.
ex.e08.hint: The rook cuts too. Think about separating the black king from its pawn, and then about who gets there first.
ex.e08.solution: 1.Rh5! The rook cuts the black king off along the fifth rank. The pawn goes down on its own: 1...c3, 2.Ke2! (the only move), 2...c2 and 3.Rh1 (the only move), and your king reaches it. 1.Ke2 at once also holds. What loses is putting the rook in front of the pawn: 1.Rc1? Kc5, and the black king escorts the pawn. The idea comes from Yuri61's study.
ex.e13: White to play and draw. A central pawn, and your rook is already in front of it. Waiting loses.
ex.e13.hint: First drive the black king away from the pawn. Then, every move, ask: check, or back in front of the pawn?
ex.e13.solution: 1.Rf1+! Kg4 and 2.Re1: the rook goes back in front of the pawn (2.Rg1+? loses). 2...Kf4 3.Rf1+, 3...Ke4 4.Re1+ and, when the king abandons the pawn with 4...Kf3, 5.Rxe5. Every move is the only one: check when the king leans on the pawn, go back when it steps away.
ex.e14: White to play and draw. A bishop pawn, and the black rook on e5 cuts your king off. From Emms's position, with the analysis in GothamMath's study.
ex.e14.hint: Your king cannot stay far from the e-file. What does the black rook have to watch?
ex.e14.solution: 1.Kd4! The king attacks the rook and wins the tempo it needs. 1...Re4+ 2.Kd3: the king stays close, and the black rook has gone back in front. Now the checks: 2...Kg4 3.Rg1+, 3...Kf3 4.Rf1+. Every move is the only one. Any other first move loses: your king stays too far and the black rook has time.
ex.e15: White to play and draw. A knight pawn, your king cut off by two files. Chéron, 1923: with a central pawn this would lose. Here the black king's lack of room saves you, if you find the moves.
ex.e15.hint: Your king wants to get close to the c-file, and the rook stays in front of the pawn. When the black rook offers itself, look at what is left.
ex.e15.solution: 1.Ke4! (the only move) 1...Kc6 2.Rc1+ (2.Ra1, 2.Re1, 2.Rf1, 2.Rg1 and 2.Rh1 also hold) 2...Rc5 3.Rb1! Rc3 4.Kd4! Ra3 5.Rc1+ Kb6 6.Rc3! The rook offers itself: if 6...Rxc3, your king takes and the knight pawn does not get through. Chéron's position, 1923.
key.front: Knight pawn, white king cut off by one file: the white rook goes in front of the pawn and checks from the front, or offers a trade. A draw, whoever moves.
key.emms: Bishop pawn, same distance: here it depends on the move. With Black to play, the black king marches forward and wins; with White to play, the defence still arrives in time.
key.bpawn: White king cut off by two files: the rook goes in front of the pawn and from there checks without stopping. Only that route holds.
key.tal: Tal against Zaitsev, Riga, 1968: the white rook is far from the first rank and has to get back before the king moves. Tal moved the king first and lost.
key.arencibia: Arencibia against Vladimirov, Leon, 1991: the white king has to get close to the black rook to attack it. Arencibia moved the rook instead and lost.
key.side: The pawn is already close to promoting: the white rook does not go in front of it, but separates the black king from the pawn, and the white king does the rest.
key.capa: The white rook is far from the pawn, but still in time: it starts checking right now and does not stop until it is in front of the pawn.
history: When the defending king is cut off from the pawn, it cannot stop the pawn by itself, and the rook has to do the job: it goes in front of the pawn and checks from the front, or offers itself for a trade at the right moment. It is one of the classical defences against rook and pawn, and it works better against some pawns than others: against a knight pawn it usually holds, against a bishop pawn it depends on who is to move. André Chéron was already showing this in 1923, and Edmar Mednis and John Emms set out the practical rules in more recent books. Capablanca showed the other side: if the rook arrives late, the checks no longer help.
practice: Practical challenge: a knight pawn, your king cut off by one file. Rook in front of the pawn, checks from the front and the trade at the right moment. The goal is a draw.
